games.title: Tunnels & Trolls
games.note: Phoenix librarian Ken St. Andre wrote it in 1975 after finding the D&D rules confusing; it uses only six-sided dice.

games.title: GURPS
games.note: The Generic Universal RolePlaying System: one rules set for any genre. Fallout was first built on it.

games.title: Dungeon (1975)
games.note: Don Daglow wrote this unlicensed take on D&D on a PDP-10 at Pomona College.

games.title: Wizardry: Proving Grounds of the Mad Overlord
games.note: Its first-person random battles became the model for Dragon Quest's combat, and the series stayed popular in Japan for decades.

games.title: Ultima II: The Revenge of the Enchantress
games.note: Published by Sierra On-Line with a cloth map in the box, which became an Ultima tradition.

games.title: Ultima III: Exodus
games.note: The first release of Origin Systems, the company Richard Garriott founded with his brother and father to publish it.

games.title: Ultima IV: Quest of the Avatar
games.note: Instead of slaying a villain, you win by living up to eight virtues such as honesty and compassion.

games.title: Ultima V: Warriors of Destiny
games.note: A ruler twists the eight virtues into harsh laws, so the player becomes a rebel against forced morality.

games.title: Ultima VI: The False Prophet
games.note: The gargoyles you fight turn out to have their own side of the story, and their own prophecy about you.

games.title: Ultima VII: The Black Gate
games.note: Almost every object can be picked up or used; it introduced the pop-up container windows known as 'gumps'.

games.title: Ultima Underworld II: Labyrinth of Worlds
games.note: Looking Glass then ported and extended its engine to build System Shock.

games.title: The Bard's Tale
games.note: The first computer RPG other than Wizardry to challenge the Ultima series in sales; set in the town of Skara Brae.

games.title: Might and Magic Book One: The Secret of the Inner Sanctum
games.note: Jon Van Caneghem wrote the Apple II version almost single-handedly over three years.

games.title: Pool of Radiance
games.note: The first official Advanced Dungeons & Dragons computer game; its engine powered SSI's 'Gold Box' series.

games.title: Curse of the Azure Bonds
games.note: Players could carry their Pool of Radiance characters over into it.

games.title: Eye of the Beholder
games.note: Westwood made it for SSI as a real-time AD&D dungeon crawl beneath the city of Waterdeep.

games.title: Lands of Lore: The Throne of Chaos
games.note: Westwood's own dungeon RPG world; Patrick Stewart voices King Richard in the CD-ROM version.

games.title: Legend of Grimrock
games.note: Made by four founders in Espoo, Finland; the project began back in 2001 as a Dungeon Master clone.

games.title: Darklands
games.note: Set in 15th-century Germany, where saints, alchemy and witches work the way people of the time believed.

games.title: Wasteland
games.note: Its rules came from Michael Stackpole's tabletop game Mercenaries, Spies and Private Eyes; Stackpole also wrote for it.

games.title: Starflight
games.note: You run a starship crew, exploring, mining and trading across hundreds of planets.

games.title: Star Control
games.note: Paired a light strategy layer with two-player arcade duels between very different alien ships.

games.title: Star Control II
games.note: Its code was released in 2002 and lives on as the free remake The Ur-Quan Masters.

games.title: Space Rogue
games.note: Paul Neurath's blend of a 2D tile RPG and 3D space flight; its royalties helped fund Ultima Underworld.

games.title: Legends of Valour
games.note: A free-roaming first-person RPG set entirely inside one walled city.

games.title: Neverwinter Nights (1991)
games.note: The first graphical MMORPG, run on AOL from 1991 to 1997 on SSI's Gold Box engine.

links.took: Fantasy dungeon adventuring from the D&D games Garriott ran at home as a teenager.
links.added: A first-person wireframe dungeon on the Apple II, food to manage and quests from Lord British.

src.t: Wikipedia: Akalabeth: World of Doom (Garriott 'primarily inspired by Dungeons & Dragons')

links.extra: Garriott also borrowed names from Tolkien, such as the Balrog.

links.took: D&D-style classes, races and alignments, and a party exploring a monster-filled dungeon.
links.added: A six-character party mapping a ten-level wireframe maze on a home computer.

src.t: Wikipedia: Wizardry: Proving Grounds of the Mad Overlord

links.extra: Wikipedia calls it one of the first D&D-style role-playing games written for computers.

links.took: The PLATO dungeon crawl's party-based exploration of a first-person maze.
links.added: Brought the format to home computers and sold it in stores.

src.t: Wikipedia: Wizardry: Proving Grounds of the Mad Overlord

links.extra: Wikipedia says Wizardry drew on PLATO games, most notably Oubliette (1977).

links.took: D&D's stats, character classes and dungeon adventures.
links.added: Simpler, cheaper rules using only six-sided dice and a points-based magic system.

src.t: Wikipedia: Tunnels & Trolls (Ken St. Andre)

links.extra: St. Andre wrote it after finding the D&D rules confusing; Jon Freeman later called it a cheaper, simpler D&D.

links.took: D&D's party of adventurers, monsters and treasure.
links.added: Turned them into a program on a university PDP-10 mainframe.

src.t: Wikipedia: Dungeon (1975 video game)

links.extra: An unlicensed adaptation written by Don Daglow at Pomona College.

links.took: Fighters, wizards and clerics: Henk Rogers wanted 'a full Dungeons & Dragons game'.
links.added: A Japanese-language RPG that introduced the genre to Japan and sold about 150,000 copies.

src.t: Henk Rogers, interview, Time Extension (Simon Parkin), Dec 2023

links.took: Wizardry's first-person dungeon crawl, which Rogers saw had no equivalent in Japan.
links.added: Character appearance options and health shown as a colored bar, aimed at players new to RPGs.

src.t: Henk Rogers, interview, Time Extension (Simon Parkin), Dec 2023
MobyGames: The Black Onyx trivia

links.extra: Rogers: 'The US had Ultima and Wizardry. But there were no such adventures in Japan.'

links.took: First-person random battles; Yuji Horii and Koichi Nakamura discovered Wizardry at a Macworld expo.
links.added: Overhead exploration and simple menu battles for Famicom players new to role-playing.

src.t: Wikipedia: Dragon Quest (cites Yuji Horii, 1UP.com interview)

links.extra: Horii: 'I personally was playing Wizardry and Ultima at the time.'

links.took: Ultima's overhead view of the world map.
links.added: A single hero, menu-driven battles and a gentle difficulty curve for console players.

src.t: Wikipedia: Dragon Quest (cites Yuji Horii)

links.extra: Horii said 'Ultima' in general, not one specific game.

links.took: Party-based dungeon exploration and turn-based battles from early computer RPGs.
links.added: Four customizable heroes on a console, side-view battles and a story built around crystals.

src.t: Wikipedia: Wizardry: Proving Grounds of the Mad Overlord

links.extra: Wikipedia credits Wizardry, together with Ultima, as an inspiration for both Dragon Quest and Final Fantasy.

links.took: Party-based, first-person dungeon crawling, improving on Wizardry, which Michael Cranford felt fell short.
links.added: Color graphics, animated monster portraits and a bard whose songs work as party-wide spells.

src.t: Wikipedia: The Bard's Tale (cites Michael Cranford)

links.extra: On some computers players could import characters from Wizardry and Ultima III.

links.took: Most of the design came from Michael Cranford and Brian Fargo's own D&D sessions.
links.added: A whole town, Skara Brae, to explore street by street, with dungeons below.

src.t: Wikipedia: The Bard's Tale (cites Michael Cranford)

links.took: The first-person party dungeon crawl that Wizardry popularized.
links.added: A large world of towns, castles and outdoor areas instead of one dungeon.
links.extra: Genre link only; no documented statement from Jon Van Caneghem about Wizardry.

links.took: The Might and Magic name, world and fantasy creatures.
links.added: A turn-based strategy spin-off about hero-led armies capturing towns and mines.

src.t: Wikipedia: Heroes of Might and Magic

links.extra: Its gameplay descends more directly from New World Computing's King's Bounty (1990).

links.took: Lord British, the tile-based overworld and first-person dungeons.
links.added: Time travel through Earth's history, a bigger world and a cloth map in the box.

src.t: Wikipedia: Ultima II: The Revenge of the Enchantress

links.took: The Ultima overworld, towns and dungeons.
links.added: A party of four with classes and races, and tactical turn-based battles on their own screen.

src.t: Wikipedia: Ultima III: Exodus

links.took: Party play, Britannia's towns and Ultima III's tactical combat.
links.added: A quest to become a moral example: the eight virtues replace killing a big villain.

src.t: Wikipedia: Ultima IV: Quest of the Avatar

links.extra: Garriott was partly prompted by letters from parents upset that his earlier games rewarded immoral play.

links.took: Britannia, the Avatar and the eight virtues.
links.added: A darker story in which a ruler enforces the virtues as harsh laws.

src.t: Wikipedia: Ultima V: Warriors of Destiny

links.took: Britannia, the Avatar and townspeople who keep daily routines.
links.added: One continuous world map and a story that asks who the real enemy is.

src.t: Wikipedia: Ultima VI: The False Prophet

links.took: Ultima VI's seamless world full of objects you can handle.
links.added: A world where almost anything can be moved or used, and pop-up 'gump' inventory windows.

src.t: Wikipedia: Ultima VII: The Black Gate

links.took: Britannia and the 'gump' container windows that Ultima VII introduced.
links.added: Put that world online for thousands of players at once.

src.t: Wikipedia: Ultima VII: The Black Gate

links.extra: Wikipedia notes the gump interface carried over into Ultima VIII, Ultima IX and Ultima Online.

links.took: Ultima's overhead exploration of a large world.
links.added: Moved it to a post-nuclear American desert patrolled by a squad of Desert Rangers.

src.t: Wikipedia: Wasteland (cites Brian Fargo, MicroTimes, 1987)

links.extra: Fargo called it 'a hybrid of the Ultima series and The Bard's Tale', naming the series rather than Ultima IV.

links.took: Interplay's Bard's Tale-style party combat, which Brian Fargo said it resembled.
links.added: More strategy in combat, plus skills and a map that explosions could change.

src.t: Wikipedia: Wasteland (cites Brian Fargo, MicroTimes, 1987)

links.extra: Both were made at Interplay with Brian Fargo in charge.

links.took: Mechanics influenced by Tunnels & Trolls, whose creator Ken St. Andre co-designed Wasteland.
links.added: A post-apocalyptic setting and skill system built mainly on Mercenaries, Spies and Private Eyes.

src.t: Wikipedia: Wasteland (video game)

links.extra: St. Andre also pitched Wasteland's killer-robot storyline.

links.took: Official Advanced D&D rules, monsters and the Forgotten Realms setting.
links.added: The first licensed AD&D computer game, with tactical turn-based battles on a grid.

src.t: Wikipedia: Pool of Radiance

links.extra: TSR designers wrote the scenario and SSI programmers coded it.

links.took: The Gold Box engine, the AD&D rules and your old party, which could be imported.
links.added: A new Forgotten Realms story about magical sigils binding the heroes.

src.t: Wikipedia: Pool of Radiance

links.took: SSI's Gold Box engine and AD&D rules.
links.added: Put them online through AOL so many players could share one world.

src.t: Wikipedia: Pool of Radiance

links.extra: Wikipedia notes the engine was reused for 'the Neverwinter Nights online game'.

links.took: Don Daglow's early idea of D&D on a computer.
links.added: A graphical online version, made 16 years later at Daglow's company Stormfront Studios.

src.t: Wikipedia: Neverwinter Nights (1991 video game)

links.extra: Daglow wrote Dungeon as a student and later led Neverwinter Nights at Stormfront, which he founded.

links.took: Dungeon Master's real-time, square-by-square first-person dungeon with hands-on inventory.
links.added: Official AD&D rules and Forgotten Realms lore beneath the city of Waterdeep.

src.t: Wikipedia: Eye of the Beholder

links.extra: Wikipedia says its design and gameplay are similar to Dungeon Master; Computer Gaming World's reviewer said so too.

links.took: Westwood's real-time first-person dungeon design from its two Eye of the Beholder games.
links.added: Its own fantasy world, an automap and a voiced story with Patrick Stewart as the king.

src.t: Wikipedia: Eye of the Beholder

links.extra: SSI made Eye of the Beholder III in-house; Westwood went on to create Lands of Lore.

links.took: Square-by-square real-time dungeon crawling; the project began as a Dungeon Master clone.
links.added: Modern 3D graphics and a single, puzzle-packed dungeon made by four founders in Finland.

src.t: Wikipedia: Legend of Grimrock (cites Petri Häkkinen, 2011)

links.extra: Häkkinen: 'no longer a clone but an original game (strongly) inspired by DM.'

links.took: A four-character party moving square by square through a real-time dungeon.
links.added: Hand-built puzzles, traps and secret switches instead of D&D rules.

src.t: Wikipedia: Legend of Grimrock (cites a 2011 developer post)

links.extra: The developers named Eye of the Beholder and Ultima Underworld on their website in 2011.

links.took: The atmosphere of a first-person 3D dungeon full of secrets.
links.added: Kept old-school square-by-square movement instead of free movement.

src.t: Wikipedia: Legend of Grimrock (cites a 2011 developer post)

links.took: A large medieval world built on skills and history rather than heroic fantasy.
links.added: A vast, procedurally generated region seen in first-person 3D.

src.t: Wikipedia: Darklands (cites Todd Howard)

links.extra: Todd Howard credited Darklands as an influence on The Elder Scrolls in general, not on Daggerfall alone.

links.took: An open galaxy of planets to explore, alien races to meet and resources to mine.
links.added: Funny, character-driven alien conversations and Star Control's arcade ship duels.

src.t: Wikipedia: Star Control II (cites Paul Reiche III and Fred Ford, GDC 2015)

links.extra: Reiche and Ford said they drew heavily on Starflight once they had the idea.

links.took: The ship roster and arcade ship-to-ship combat.
links.added: A story-driven open galaxy, where the first game's lore lived mostly in the manual.

src.t: Wikipedia: Star Control II (cites Fred Ford)

links.extra: Ford said they 'made a conscious decision to tell more of a story.'

links.took: Paul Neurath's mix of RPG and simulation, which he felt was jarring in Space Rogue.
links.added: One immersive real-time 3D dungeon, partly funded by Space Rogue royalties.

src.t: Wikipedia: Ultima Underworld (cites Paul Neurath)

links.took: The real-time 3D engine, the Avatar and simulation-driven dungeons.
links.added: A bigger adventure across several linked worlds, starting from a trapped castle.

src.t: Wikipedia: Ultima Underworld II: Labyrinth of Worlds

links.took: Free-form first-person roaming through a city full of things to do.
links.added: Stretched that freedom across a whole continent, Tamriel, with generated dungeons.

src.t: Wikipedia: The Elder Scrolls: Arena (cites Ted Peterson)

links.extra: Peterson described Legends of Valour as a free-form first-person game set in a single city.

links.took: First-person 3D dungeons you explore freely in real time.
links.added: A huge open continent with towns, quests and dungeons between them.

src.t: Wikipedia: The Elder Scrolls: Arena

links.extra: Designers Ted Peterson, Vijay Lakshman and Julian LeFay were fans; Wikipedia calls Underworld their main inspiration.
